segments.text: The cloud sounds harmless, right? Until a giant data centre moves next door. Suddenly, it's personal.
Behind the AI boom are real buildings, using land, power, and other resources.
The International Energy Agency expects data-centre electricity use to roughly double from twenty twenty-five to twenty thirty.
So neighbours are asking: can our grid cope? And who's paying for those new power lines?
Some cooling systems use water, depending on their design and location. In dry regions, that matters.
Others worry about noise from cooling equipment and backup generators near their homes.
From Mexico to South Africa, communities have demanded clearer answers about projects on their doorstep.
Of course, data centres run useful services. Supporters point to investment and tax revenue. Those benefits matter, too.
But so does the deal: transparent resource use, noise controls, fair costs, and residents involved before construction starts.
The cloud may be global. Its neighbours aren't. If the future's moving next door, shouldn't they get a say?
